overview: Two mobile genetic elements that can persist in a bacterial cell, distinguished by their origin as a virus versus an independent extrachromosomal circle of DNA.
genZNote: Prophage: a virus napping inside your genome. Plasmid: DNA that just moved in as a roommate.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: The genome of a temperate bacteriophage integrated into (or existing as an episome within) the host bacterial chromosome during lysogeny.
aspects.valueB: A small, typically circular, extrachromosomal DNA molecule that replicates independently of the bacterial chromosome.

aspects.label: Origin
aspects.valueA: Derived from a bacteriophage that infected the cell and entered the lysogenic cycle instead of lysing it.
aspects.valueB: Not viral in origin — an independently evolved genetic element, though some plasmids can be mobilized like phages.

aspects.label: Replication
aspects.valueA: Replicates passively along with the host chromosome while integrated; can excise and replicate as a phage during induction.
aspects.valueB: Replicates independently using its own origin of replication, sometimes at high copy number.

aspects.label: Genes Often Carried
aspects.valueA: Phage structural/lysis genes plus sometimes toxin genes (lysogenic conversion, e.g. diphtheria or Shiga toxin).
aspects.valueB: Antibiotic resistance genes, virulence factors, or metabolic genes (e.g. F plasmid, R plasmids).

aspects.label: Transfer Mechanism
aspects.valueA: Spread via transduction when the prophage excises and packages into new phage particles.
aspects.valueB: Spread via conjugation (if conjugative) or transformation.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: Viral genome integrated in the host; can trigger lysis.
aspects.valueB: Independent extrachromosomal DNA circle; not derived from a virus.
